question: The shipwreck that took place on 26 February 2023 at Steccato di Cutro resulted in the deaths of at least 94 people, including numerous children. Witness reports from survivors, media reports and judicial developments have raised questions regarding the timeliness of the rescue operation and the coordination between relevant authorities.

The victims’ families are calling for truth and justice, a full investigation into who was responsible, guarantees that they will be able to participate in the legal proceedings – including through the issuance of the necessary visas – and measures to ensure that such tragedies do not happen again.
In the light of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and international obligations regarding search and rescue at sea, the Commission is asked: 1.
Does it consider that the obligations arising from EU and international law regarding search and rescue were complied with in the Cutro case?
Does it intend to call for an independent assessment of the operational coordination and any shortcomings that may have emerged?

What measures could it take to help ensure that the victims’ families are guaranteed effective access to justice, including by facilitating the issuance of the necessary visas to enable them to participate in legal proceedings in the Member States?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) The Commission deeply regrets the tragic loss of lives in the shipwreck of Steccato di Cutro. Rendering assistance to persons in distress at sea is a moral duty and a legal obligation under international law. Migrant deaths at sea are a tragic reminder of the need for a comprehensive approach to migration management and countering migrant smuggling.

Under international maritime law, responsibility for coordinating search and rescue operations lies primarily with the competent national authorities. It is for the competent national authorities, including judicial authorities where appropriate, to establish the facts and assess compliance with the applicable legal framework.

The Commission continues to monitor developments within the limits of the competences conferred by the Treaties. The Commission has no competence to request an independent assessment of an individual search and rescue operation carried out by a Member State. The Victims’ Rights Directive1, revised in June 20262, provides for a comprehensive set of rights for victims of crime and their family members3.

It is for national authorities to ensure their application in the specific circumstances raised by the Honourable Member, in line also with the principle of access to justice as enshrined in Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union4. The examination and issuance of visas fall within the competence of the Member States, as laid down in applicable EU law5.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2012/29/oj/eng. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2026/1472/oj. 3 In its role of Guardian of the Treaties, the Commission closely monitors the transposition and implementation
of these rules by the Member States. 4 Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union [2012] OJ C326/391, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/treaty/char_2012/oj.

5 Regulation (EC) No 810/2009 establishing a Community Code on Visas (Visa Code) and Regulation (EU) 2018/1806 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 November 2018 listing the third countries whose nationals must be in possession of visas when crossing the external borders and those whose nationals are exempt from that requirement (codification) (Visa Regulation).
